what_it_does: CXL (Compute Express Link) is a relatively new high-speed cable-and-protocol standard that lets a server plug in extra memory chips as if they were ordinary main memory, even though they are physically on a separate card connected through a slot on the motherboard. The catch is that fetching data from CXL memory takes 140 to 410 nanoseconds longer than fetching from the server's built-in memory — a small but meaningful gap for latency-sensitive workloads. Until now, engineers have had little systematic data on exactly how, why, and when that latency penalty hurts real applications. Melody is a measurement framework that ran 265 workloads across four real CXL devices and five different server types, varying injected latency levels to tease apart the different sources of slowdown. Its key methodological contribution is SPA (Sub-operation Performance Analysis), which breaks a single memory access into its component steps and measures each one separately, pinpointing exactly where in the request pipeline CXL adds delay. Melody also produces the first published measurements of CXL tail latency (the slowest outlier requests) and shows where the CPU's built-in data prefetcher — a circuit that tries to fetch data before it is needed — succeeds and fails under CXL's higher latency.
